MA4344 overview

MA4344 Topic Guide

Subgroups and Lagrange's Theorem

Turn subgroup information into divisibility and order conclusions.

Purpose

Use subgroup tests and Lagrange's theorem efficiently in the recurring finite-group proof style.Exam use: Operation, nonempty/subgroup test, sizes, index/cosets and the exact divisibility implication are shown.

Question plan

  1. State whether the group is finite and identify the subgroup.
  2. Apply |H| divides |G|, or use the order of an element via ⟨g⟩.
  3. List only consequences justified by divisibility.
  4. For a matrix-parametrised set, first prove closure and identify the parameter map.
  5. Question interpretation: For subgroup, apply a one-step test; for order conclusions, use Lagrange in the correct direction; for cyclic subgroups, distinguish element order from group order.

Key terms

Subgroup, cyclic subgroup ⟨g⟩, order |g|, index [G:H], left coset. Lagrange: if H≤G and G is finite, then |H| divides |G| and |G|=[G:H]|H|.Rapid recall: Nonempty H is a subgroup iff ab^{-1} in H for all a,b in H. For finite G, |H| divides |G| and ord(g) divides |G|; converses generally fail.

Proof method

Partition G into left cosets of H; multiplication by a representative bijects H with each coset, so every coset has |H| elements. For an element g, apply this to ⟨g⟩.Exam workflow: Check nonemptiness, closure under ab^{-1}, then use coset partitions to justify divisibility and compute indices.

Worked simple proof

Claim: an element of a group of order 15 cannot have order 6. Since |g|=|⟨g⟩| divides 15 by Lagrange, 6∤15. Contradiction.

Practice 1 — subgroup and cosets in Z12 [8 marks]

Prompt. Show H={0,4,8} is a subgroup of additive Z12, and find its order, index, cosets and the order of 4. Question-demand diagnosis. Give a subgroup proof before numerical conclusions. Fastest route. Use the one-step difference test, then list representatives 0,1,2,3. Topic-specific trap. In additive notation use a−b, not an unadapted multiplicative inverse argument.

In Z12 under addition, H={0,4,8}. It is nonempty and for a,b in H, a-b is again a multiple of 4 mod 12, so H<=Z12. Its order is 3 and index 4. The cosets are H,1+H,2+H,3+H. Element 4 has order 3 since 3*4=0 mod 12 and no smaller positive multiple vanishes.

Graduated exam bridge

1. If |G|=42, list possible orders of an element. Check: positive divisors of 42 only.

2. Let H={[[1,n],[0,1]]:n∈Z}. Prove H≤SL(2,Z) and show H≅Z. Check: multiply matrices to add parameters; n↦matrix(n) is an isomorphism.

Practice 2 — a point stabiliser in S4 [8 marks]

Prompt. Prove K={σ∈S4:σ(4)=4} is a subgroup and find its order and index. Question-demand diagnosis. Link the stabiliser condition to closure and then to S3. Fastest route. Use ab⁻¹ fixing 4 and restrict permutations to {1,2,3}. Topic-specific trap. Fixing one point leaves 3!, not 4!, permissible permutations.

Paper-style synthesis: show K={sigma in S4:sigma(4)=4} is a subgroup and find its order/index. Check ab^{-1} fixes 4 when a,b do; restriction to {1,2,3} gives K isomorphic to S3, so |K|=6 and index 4.

Mistakes

  • Claiming every divisor of |G| is realised as an element order.
  • Using Lagrange before establishing subgroup status.
  • Confusing the order of G, H and an element.
  • Recovery rule: Lagrange says subgroup order must divide group order, not that every divisor occurs as a subgroup order.

Checklist

  • I can state Lagrange with its hypotheses.
  • I can use cyclic subgroups for element-order claims.
  • I can prove a parametrised matrix set is a subgroup.
  • Final 60-second audit: Operation, nonempty/subgroup test, sizes, index/cosets and the exact divisibility implication are shown.

Past-paper note

High confidence: Lagrange and the matrix-subgroup pattern occur in both 2023/24 and 2024/25. Back to paper evidence.
